📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Vice City portal Easter egg is a unique event in Grand Theft Auto 6 that lets you travel through time. It might not look like it, but the existence of a secret portal in Leonida is quite plausible, considering the UFOs appearing in the skies and the forgotten haunted hotels you can visit.

To experience this event and open the portal, you will have to complete a long series of steps. But don't worry, below, we explain everything you need to know to complete the Vice City portal Easter egg in GTA 6.

If you want to start the Vice City portal event in GTA 6, you must travel to Key Lento, the initial area in the game, and head to the Badger radio tower, northeast of the Nifty Threads Island Wear shop. Enter the tower and climb to the top to reach what appears to be a control room.

Beside the door, there's a lever. Pull it up then press the button on the panel near the old television. If you've done everything correctly, the TV will turn on and display the word "Malibu." Now, leave the tower and prepare for the next step.

Sources indicate that after you have finished the initial ratio tower step, you will need to visit 12 LPL substations around Leonidas following a specific order. There will be a letter or two on the outer wall of each substation, which will form a secret message when all 12 letters are put together. In each one, you will find either a button or a lever that represents a letter or symbol. To ensure you're interacting with the correct one, check the pink tape near the button/lever and look for the letter/symbol it features.

Recent findings suggest that before you start, keep in mind that you can't fast travel using the RydeMe app or swap between characters. Doing so resets the mission, and you will need to return to the radio tower to start it again. You'll know that you have completed this step when you receive a message from an unknown contact after you pull up the last lever. Below, we listed the substations in the order you must visit them, where you will find the button or lever you must activate, and which letter they represent.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — Southwest corner of Downtown, just southwest of Zenith gym.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — West side of Balsero, just northwest of Randy's shop.

Location: Key Lento (Mariana County) —Northwest of Kenton's shop.

Location: Vice Beach (Vice-Dale County) — North side of Penmarch Isle.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — West side of Bayside, just northwest of the Vice City apartment.

Location: Port Gellhorn (Kelly County) — North of Moses' shop.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) — East of Big Shot Ammu-Nation shop​​​​​​​.

Location: Vice City (Vice-Dale County) — Northwest area of Gloriana Key.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) - East side of Hamlet, just northeast of the Boone Speedway.

Location: Gellhorn (Kelly County) — Northeast of Raceway.

Location: Hamlet (Vice-Dale County) - South side of Hamlet, just southeast of Boone Speedway and the Pay 'N' Spray.

Location: North Mariana County (Mariana County) — South of Breakwater Quarry.

If you combine all the letters, you'll get the message: Life is passing me by, which is a PC cheat code that allows you to speed up time in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.

The final step in the event requires you to follow the instructions in the message you receive after activating the 12th lever: head to the T. H. Power Station, east of Hamlet in Vice-Dale County, between 7 p.m. and 6 a.m. Once there, you will find the portal that will take you to the original Vice City.

You can find the portal on the north side of the power station. You'll know you're at the right place if you can see traces of energy from the portal running through the cables in the area. Reaching the portal might be difficult, considering how heavily guarded the area is. Consider either using a helicopter or swimming around the area to find a good entry point.

Recent findings suggest that once you find the portal, pull the lever on the left side of the gate, and you'll be teleported. To leave the original Vice City, just head to the room behind the bar, and you will be back to the world of GTA 6. By completing this event, you will receive Tony Vercetti's Hawaiian shirt, the American Glory motorcycle (don't forget to register it!), and unlock a upcoming livery for purchase at Vice Vinyl.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial.

  • In a recent development, the scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial. In her storytelling, Coburn shares with her subject a talent for distilling complex ideas and expressing them with force and clarity; the result is a movie that fully honors the breadth and depth of Du Bois’ achievements as a groundbreaking Black writer, historian, and activist.

According to recent reports, one of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works. Related Stories ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’.

In a recent development, the scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives. “Rita and I talked about what types of touchstones we needed to define the narrative musically,” Bostic told IndieWire. “There was the regional touchstone, the era-specific touchstone, the interior emotional aspects that we wanted to heighten with music. Then there’s always the discovery process as you begin to create.”.

For Bostic, that discovery process is one of the most exciting aspects of film composing. While she had a number of reference points as she began work on the score, she soon found herself following intuition to take them in different directions than initially intended. “There’s always what I call the hands-on-the-clay moment,” Bostic said. “You have your list, and you have your frame of reference, but the process is fluid.”.

According to Coburn, Bostic’s ability to bring a historical perspective to her scores made her an ideal collaborator for the film. “Kathryn pulled from the region of Great Barrington [where Du Bois was born] as well as Latest York in that time period, and then what was happening with the African-American community that Du Bois was entering,” Coburn remarked. “There wasn’t gospel then, so you were looking at a small group of Black people going to the churches there in New England. What were they listening to, and therefore what was he listening to?”.

Bostic drew on the music of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a Black a capella ensemble that inspired Du Bois, but then moved in a completely different direction to explore his time in Berlin, when he encountered and fell in love with classical music. She also incorporated Wolof music from Senegal and the Gambia in collaboration with Coburn’s daughter, who studied classical music and worked in the music department on “Rebel with a Cause.”.

It has been revealed that “She found a Senegalese professor online who worked with her so she could sing the Wolof,” Coburn said. “Kathryn and I agreed that we had to put the Wolof in the film because it connects Du Bois to his Ghanaian roots. But we had to find it, and we wanted it to be as authentic as possible.”.

In a recent development, for Bostic, the challenge was taking an audience from 2026 and presenting the music in a way that would recreate the way in which Du Bois experienced it over a hundred years earlier. “There’s the historic arc of the times, as well as what he’s experiencing emotionally,” Bostic said. In the places where her score was informed by spirituals and the work of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the composer tried to tie the emotional subtext to the context in which she knew Du Bois was consuming the music.

According to recent reports, “When he went to Fisk University, his mother had recently died,” Bostic stated. “So that music was a wellspring for his grieving, and I think that depth of sorrow and the catharsis that resulted from that sorrow inspired the sort of deep self-reflection that became such a deep part of who he was. That self-reflection led to a basic decency and humanity, and even now I think of him as being light years ahead of people in the way he embodied justice. I want to shine a light on that.”.

It has been revealed that coburn felt a similar sense of purpose, especially since the more she dug into Du Bois’ life the more she realized how relevant his insights were to America in 2026. “He speaks to this current time,” Coburn noted, adding that the importance of Du Bois’ work gave her own work a sense of urgency and responsibility. “I knew that it might be 20 or 30 years before we get another Du Bois documentary. I hope not, but I looked at his life and knew that I had to do the best job that I could. We did everything we could for Du Bois because we felt he had done everything he could for us.”.

The greatness of “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is that it brings the viewer into Du Bois’ perspective as his world view continues to expand over a 95-year life, and the music is a major part of that subjectivity.

“Kathryn understands that music is a character in any documentary, and her music embodies the character of W.E.B. Du Bois,” Coburn remarked. “ In the music, we had to grow with him. We had to expand with him. We had to see that his love of Rembrandt and his understanding of classical music, of music that came from an Asian culture, that all of that was key to him. We were catching up with him, and he was driving us.”.

“W.E.B. DuBois: Rebel with a Cause” is right now streaming on the PBS app and website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that suzanne Collins is the engine that drives the "Hunger Games" franchise. As the author behind the books, none of the movies happen without her. Beyond that, though, Collins has remained very close to the adaptations of her work, with Lionsgate consulting with her every step of the way. That's especially true with the franchise's latest prequel film, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" — so much so that it resulted in a unique credit we rarely see in movies.

It has been revealed that "Sunrise on the Reaping" ruled the box office on its opening weekend, meaning that quite a few people might have noticed that once the credits roll, there's some text reading, "Adaptation by Suzanne Collins." So, while Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie are credited with the movie's screenplay, Collins got credit for the adaptation of her 2024 book of the same name. This is exceptionally rare in Hollywood.

"In the interest of avoiding a multiplicity of credits, the Guild is opposed to the general use of the 'Adaptation by' credit," the Writers Guild of America's screen credits manual states. But that doesn't mean it never gets used, and "Sunrise on the Reaping" warranted its rare usage. The manual further explains:.

"The Guild recognizes that there are certain unusual cases where credit is due a writer who shapes the direction of screenplay construction without qualifying for 'Screenplay by' credit. In those special cases, and only as a result of arbitration, the 'Adaptation by' credit may be used.".

Who gets credit for a screenplay can be difficult to actually pin down. In the movie business, it's rare that it's literally just one person writing a script and that's that. It's why Joss Whedon wasn't credited for his writing work on "Speed." It's also why Collins nabbed this unique credit.

Arbitration is a process used primarily to determine writing credits. As the WGA manual states, arbitration is usually the only way that this "Adaptation by" credit winds up being used. That doesn't mean that things got contentious between Billy Ray, Michael Lesslie, and Suzanne Collins, it's just a unique situation.

Industry observers note that collins generally feels happy with the "Hunger Games" movie adaptations and even co-wrote the first movie personally. By all accounts, she has a good relationship with Lionsgate, director Francis Lawrence, and other key creatives. The fact that she wound up with this rare credit, if anything, reflects her level of involvement.

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter, Ray offered a window into the collaboration, explaining that he communicated very directly with Collins when it came to determining how to adapt her latest book for the screen:.

"At the very beginning of the process, I asked Suzanne, 'What is this book about for you?' She talked about the philosophy of the book: the philosophy of propaganda and implicit submission, the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, David Hume, and John Locke. And I said, 'Suzanne, what's the book about for you emotionally?' She said, 'It's about love and loss.' I said, 'Great, that's what I'm writing.' So, anything that didn't stick to that had to go.".

Industry observers note that in many cases, the writer of a book is left out in the cold when it comes to that book being turned into a movie. But not in this case. The few changes "Sunrise on the Reaping" makes to its source material don't appear to be against Collins' wishes. She was being consulted behind the scenes the whole way and was credited as such.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing firm and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

According to recent reports, at his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He demonstrates me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes.

Industry observers note that but how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image issues. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he says with a laugh.

His connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

As retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a Latest York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

It has been revealed that one might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

He quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of New England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”.

Recent findings suggest that if the self-made Fresh Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

Twilight literally predicted Robert Pattinson being James Bond btw https://t.co/eMfeaVhbhuNovember 16, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" brings back Brad Pitt as the stuntman from Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood." But he's the only major character returning for another round. That means David Fincher's follow-up with a script from Tarantino himself introduces a newly introduced ensemble of key characters, and one of them will instantly feel familiar in the film's opening sequence.

Without giving away any specific details of the flick, the Cliff Booth movie that critics are loving begins with Brad Pitt's character taking care of his duties as an employee at the New Beverly Cinema, a real-life Los Angeles movie-house that's now owned by Quentin Tarantino (though the theater in the movie is actually the Highland Theatre, owned by "Twilight" saga star Kristen Stewart). Booth keeps an eye on the film reels, refills the RC Cola syrup tank in the soda fountain, and closes up the theater when the credits roll on "Soul Brothers Die Hard!".

Sources indicate that but once the theater is closed, that's when Booth's more pressing business begins. Two men who have been waiting in a car around the corner for the theater to closer show up with a bag, and they're making some kind of exchange for cash. One of the men might be recognizable to you, and that's Joey, played by Corey Fogelmanis. If you couldn't place who that actor was, but he looked familiar, this is where you might have seen him before.

In a recent development, corey Fogelmanis most famous role might be that of the supporting character Farkle in the "Boy Meets World" spin-off/sequel series "Girl Meets World" on the Disney Channel. The series followed Riley (Rowan Blanchard), the daughter of Corey (Ben Savage) and Topanga (Danielle Fishel) from "Boy Meets World," as she navigates adolescent life, with many of the "Boy Meets World" cast members returning. By her side was her best friend Maya, played by none other than chart-topping pop star Sabrina Carpenter.

One of their other peers throughout the series was Farkle, a peculiar, nerdy character reminiscent of the character Minkus from "Boy Meets World," played by Lee Norris. Often used for comic relief, Farkle was a regular cast member on the series.

Since then, Fogelmanis has grown up considerably, and you might have seen him as a much different kind of teen in the horror movie "Ma" with Octavia Spencer. He continued to dabble in horror with a role in the Hulu Halloween movie "Carved," but he also showed his dramatic side as the lead of the coming-of-age drama "I Wish You All the Best.".

In a recent development, most recently, you've likely seen Fogelmanis as one of the titular characters in the Prime Video series "My Life with the Walter Boys." The series follows teenager Jackie Howard (Nikki Rodriguez) after a tragic accident forces her to leave her home and live with a guardian family who has nine brothers and a sister. Fogelmanis plays Nathan, one of the Walter brothers in the series, in almost all of the episodes.

Industry observers note that fogelmanis is still evolving and growing as an actor, and his role in the Cliff Booth movie will hopefully elevate his profile as a performer. Without spoiling anything, Fogelmanis' performance gives him a chance to show a bit of a darker side. There's also a bit of comedy in there too, albeit in a twisted fashion that only Fincher and Tarantino can deliver.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" hits IMAX theaters for just two weeks starting on November 25, 2026 before hitting Netflix on December 23.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The making of “Project Hail Mary” was a miracle on par with the outer space rescue mission that Ryan Gosling is tasked with pulling off. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s bestselling novel manages to be epic without ever losing its intimacy, as Gosling traverses the galaxy and saves the world with only a very lovable rock acting alongside him. The final product was a complicated blend of practical effects, on-set puppetry, and a healthy dose of VFX magic.

Recent findings suggest that incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved. The puppetry team lead by James Ortiz had to fit into very small spaces, which frequently meant they revealed up in the frames. Visual Effects Production Supervisor Mag Sarnowska and her team were tasked with removing all of the puppeteers. But as she explained during the VFX panel at IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables, it was a small price to pay for the way it enhanced Gosling’s acting performance. Related Stories The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’ ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner.

In a recent development, “It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said. “It was great to have them there, but it did not work out sometimes. Our sets were really, really tiny. Having five people there to puppet Rocky was hard sometimes. But to everyone’s point, having something there in the frame was so helpful, especially for Ryan to act to. The eyeline? That’s a real thing. Even though our Rocky didn’t have eyes, a person’s brain makes it easier to figure out where the eyes would be just by having that constant relation between Rocky and Ryan.”.

Sarnowska — who will share the Innovation Award at the IndieWire Honors with Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, and Paul Lambert — explained that having a real reference point for VFX sequences is what ultimately makes the most effects-heavy sequences feel real.

Industry observers note that “In Ryan’s space, he has to be in the xenonite glass, so having reflections, adding the glass, it was a lot of work,” she remarked. “But having that real thing, having that reference, even if we had to replace it, that was so important. Because we knew what Rocky would look like.”.

What’s Real and What’s Not in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s newly introduced limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew.
  • Recent findings suggest that I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere.
  • Sources indicate that the Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s newly introduced limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew. The show, which follows the stunning multibillion-dollar collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, starts off a bit slow, but accelerates episode by episode until its high-octane finale.

Recent findings suggest that I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere. Some of that firm’s founders and employees share similar intellectual roots to The Altruist’s protagonists; watching its fictionalized Caroline Ellison, in particular, justify astoundingly reckless behavior with her system of mathematical-optimization-of-everything felt uncannily like watching frontier labs proceed with a seemingly inexplicable appetite for risk.

Sources indicate that the Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies. (According to people involved with the project, the working title for the project was Untitled Love Story.) But as with any fictionalized account, the series takes some liberties with the characters and plot. If you’re anything like me, you want to know what exactly is fact, and what is fiction.

Recent findings suggest that I spoke with Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, two of the reporters who exposed the FTX fiasco in real time, and who consulted on the series. “When Jen and I started working with Graham Moore, the showrunner, he made it really clear that he wanted this to be very character driven. Nobody wants an eight-hour lecture on how the blockchain works,” Dugan tells me.

Recent findings suggest that “The bones of the show are rooted in reality,” states Wieczner. Understanding these flawed and complicated characters helps explain “how one decision leads to another decision and a small oopsies turns into a multibillion-dollar fraud and this huge criminal conspiracy.”.

Even if there’s a little fiction in the nitty-gritty, Dugan states that there is one overarching truth he hopes the series will reveal: “That even the prettiest ideas still have to turn into reality through imperfect people, and those imperfect people will end up making mistakes that they cannot foresee.” Here’s what the show ripped from real life—and where it took some creative license.

CAROLINE ELLISON WROTE SEXY HARRY POTTER FAN FICTION.

Sources indicate that not quite. In the first episode, Caroline is humiliated when her raunchy writing titled “A Ride on Draco’s Nimbus” surfaces online. And while it’s true that Ellison was a huge Harry Potter fan, there is no evidence she wrote erotic fan fiction herself. Instead, this plot point is likely gesturing toward Ellison’s 2010s-era Tumblr, which was called WorldOptimisation—a reference to a 660,000-word-long work of Harry Potter fan fiction by Silicon Valley philosopher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky’s work popularized the kind of mathematically strategic thinking Ellison applies to love and business alike.

SAM TRABUCCO’S “INFINITE MONEY HACK”.

According to recent reports, in episode six, Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther) makes the mistake of introducing Sam and Caroline to a hack that proves irresistible: FTX can mint its own coin, FTT, and then allow its crypto trading firm, Alameda, to take out large loans using off-market FTT as collateral. Alameda can then use those loans to place highly leveraged, incredibly risky bets on FTX—which in turn increases the value of FTT. (TL;DR: it’s a perfect loop.) Appalling as it sounds, in real life, this practice is more or less exactly what brought SBF’s empire tumbling down.

In a recent development, “One of the things that led to the FTX bank run,” explains Wieczner, “was the leaked balance sheet that showed that much of FTX and Alameda’s holdings were in FTT, which was FTX’s own coin. So that if that went to zero, it was like a house of cards and things just would’ve fallen apart. And that’s why you see at the end why is everything is falling…you have that kind of death spiral effect.”.

In a recent development, as for Trabucco, he and his yacht (yes, it was really named Soak My Deck) didn’t get off unscathed. Trabucco didn’t face criminal charges, but was forced to liquidate many of his assets in order to help return about $80 million to defrauded investors.

CAROLINE ELLISON WAS INTO POLYAMORY.

True. Caroline chronicled some of her adventures in nonmonogamy on her since-deleted Tumblr. She once wrote, “The only acceptable style of poly is best characterized as something like ‘imperial Chinese harem.’”.

Real! In the final episode of the series, SBF presents a last-ditch plan: He wants to repurpose his early stake in Anthropic to cover the losses of billions of dollars in customer funds. Indeed, FTX did use $500 million in customer funds to purchase a 13.5% stake in Anthropic’s Series B in late 2021. Of course, Sam’s plan did not pass muster. Yet if it had, he’d have been in the clear. After the firm’s IPO last week, Alameda’s stake would be worth about $35 billion, according to The New York Times—enough to solve the disgraced firm’s liquidity issues several times over. Oh well.

CAROLINE ELLISON CONFESSED IN FRONT OF HER STAFF.

True. In the penultimate episode, a visibly cracking Caroline delivers a halting confession amidst fits of nervous giggles to a shocked staff, telling them that she knew about FTX’s shortfall of user funds that would add up to more than $8 billion. I was sure this scene had been invented, but lo and behold: Ellison did admit that she had been aware of the inappropriate transfers between the two firms at a December 2022 all-staff meeting. You can even listen to the leaked recording online.

CAROLINE ELLISON BEARS MORE RESPONSIBILITY THAN SBF.

I felt the show tilted towards placing the blame on Ellison, who is portrayed as incorrigibly risk-addicted and the muse behind SBF’s worst decisions. Constance Wang, who is played in the series by Madison Hu, is just one of the former FTX employees who found the show misrepresentative. In a lengthy X post, she rebutted its narrative: Ellison, remarked Hu, “wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the best Spock-forward episodes of the "Star Trek" franchise, "Yesteryear," is hidden deep in "Star Trek: The Animated Series." The show ran for two seasons from 1973 to 1974, and it is, in some ways, superior to "Star Trek: The Original Series." At the very least, because it's a 30-minute program, it's the more efficient show, having to tell similarly expansive sci-fi stories in half the time of "The Original Series.".

Recent findings suggest that case in point: "Yesteryear" sees Kirk (William Shatner) and Spock (Leonard Nimoy) conducting time travel experiments with the Guardian of Forever, a living, stone-like time portal previously seen in the franchise-changing "Original Series" episode "The City on the Edge of Forever." After a sojourn to the past, though, something seems to have gone wrong with causality, and history has altered. No one can remember Spock, and an Andorian man has replaced him as the first officer of the USS Enterprise. This is a new, unfamiliar timeline.

According to recent reports, kirk and Spock look up the historical records in this new timeline and find that its version of Spock died at age seven back on Vulcan, poisoned by a catlike beast called a le-matya. Spock recalls, however, being saved from the le-matya by a cousin named Selek. Upon reflection, Kirk realizes that this mysterious Selek was likely Spock, having come from the future. The pair logically deduce that Spock needs to go back in time, pose as Selek, and save his seven-year-old self from a monster.

According to recent reports, but the drama of "Yesteryear" delves deeper than a mere rescue mission. Indeed, the episode transforms into a thoughtful character piece about the decisions we make as children and the people we become as a result.

According to recent reports, spock, as you might recall, is half-human, and "Yesteryear" reveals that this was once a source of consternation for him. In fact, Spock was mocked and bullied as a child for his human blood, and he struggled between identifying as either human or Vulcan. He was once teetering on an crucial life question: will he choose the path of passionate human emotion or analytical Vulcan logic?

At age seven, the young Spock (Billy Simpson) is poised to undergo a coming-of-age ritual called the kahs-wan, a ritual that will prove his Vulcan-hood, yet he's initially unsure if he is prepared. The adult Spock gets to be present for this, and while the character is not emotional, viewers will likely wince when they see young Spock being bullied. Adult Spock has already chosen the path of logic, of course, but we can imagine his inner pain. How would you react to witnessing your own childhood bullying? Recall that adult Spock, while facing this, is also on a mission to repair time and needs to ensure that his childhood self chooses a Vulcan path. For a spell, then, he gets to be his own adult guardian.

It has been revealed that the tension of "Yesteryear" involves young Spock trekking into the desert to undergo the kahs-wan ritual a month ahead of time. He has something to prove, you see, and takes his beloved childhood pet, a bear-dog named I-Chaya, as he prepares to spend a prolonged period surviving in the desert wilderness. And while the young Spock struggles to defend himself from the local fauna, adult Spock is, luckily, nearby to protect him from a le-matya attack. Unfortunately, this leads to a very difficult decision for young Spock.

Industry observers note that during the scuffle, I-Chaya, is injured by the le-matya. A healer is then brought in and informs young Spock that although he can heal I-Chaya, it would lead to a long life full of struggle and intense pain for them. The young Spock, although caring deeply for his pet, logically deduces that euthanizing him is the logical, merciful decision.

Sources indicate that it's this decision that leads Spock toward a life of logic. He chooses the path of being a Vulcan. It's a hard-won decision, yet it allows Spock to become who he's meant to be.

"Yesteryear" was penned by D.C. Fontana, who was involved with the "Star Trek" franchise on through to the early days of "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" in the early 1990s. Fontana even went on record about how she corrected some challenges with the "Next Generation" series bible, and she is best known to Trekkies for having written classic "Original Series" episodes like "This Side of Paradise," "Journey to Babel," and "The Enterprise Incident." She also served as a story editor on "The Animated Series" and definitely had an ear for excellent sci-fi stories (having additionally contributed to the underrated Marvel animated series "Silver Surfer," and written episodes of indicates like "Earth: Final Conflict" and "ReBoot").

"Yesteryear" explores Spock's past better than any "Star Trek" episode before it, and it should be pored over by Trekkies everywhere. That it's part of the woefully under-seen "Animated Series" means that it remains largely obscure to mainstream audiences. But it needn't be, as it's readily available to watch on Paramount+. For that matter, you should watch all of "The Animate Series." Think of it as the final two years of the five-year mission from "The Original Series.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a substantial "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be noted for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Industry observers note that price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

GTA 6's Most Heartbreaking Scene Is Exactly Why You Had To Do All Those Chores

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 features as much shootin’, stealin’, and drug runnin’ as you’d expect from the latest entry in a series named after a felony.
  • Jason repairs the steps leading up to his and Lucia’s home, fixes a railing, buys groceries, orders flowers, paints the walls of their bedroom, and more to prepare for Lucia’s arrival from prison.
  • note: Spoilers for the ending of Chapter 1 follow.].
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 features as much shootin’, stealin’, and drug runnin’ as you’d expect from the latest entry in a series named after a felony. However, some players have been caught off-guard by just how much the early game is all about the more mundane parts of life. Namely, you gotta do a bunch of chores around the house. In many ways, GTA 6 is as much of an everyday life sim as it is a game about committing crimes.

Jason repairs the steps leading up to his and Lucia’s home, fixes a railing, buys groceries, orders flowers, paints the walls of their bedroom, and more to prepare for Lucia’s arrival from prison. All those chores might seem less thrilling than the opening hours you’d expect in a significant-budget action game. But it turns out they set up a tragic heartbreak I simply did not see coming.

Sources indicate that [Ed. note: Spoilers for the ending of Chapter 1 follow.].

Chapter 1 involves Jason and Lucia trying to get work from Mattia, the shady boyfriend of Kat, a mother-to-be whom Lucia befriended in prison. Part of that involves a standout sequence set to a Carly Rae Jepsen banger before Lucia gets lost in orgy central. (Vice City, y’all!) Bro, Mattia promises a job that could pay ten grand, bro. They just have to grab a bag from a locker and deliver it, bro.

It has been revealed that red flags abound, but Jason and Lucia go along for the ride, which rapidly results in their arrest. Crooked cops show up, the couple gets into a shootout, and Jason gets grievously wounded while the couple struggle to keep hold over a bag containing who knows what.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 does a great job of showing how various systems, both governmental and societal, are against Jason and Lucia, and that shines through here. In Jason and Lucia, Mattia sees a pair of not prospective partners, but a down-on-their-luck couple he can easily exploit — and they’re all too willing to play into his hands. Mattia leverages their desperation, even making them play dress up with Lucia in a platinum blonde wig and Jason in one of Mattia’s gaudy shirts, so they’d take the fall for whatever shady shit Mattia is up to. Clearly, he knew the danger surrounding this bag with shady cops and an organized outfit after it and gladly fed Jason and Lucia to the wolves.

Sources indicate that they escape, but their horrible night has only just begun. Lucia takes Jason to his friend Cal, who brings Jason — and the mysterious bag — to the hospital. (Lucia later learns the hospital took everything from the couple’s BuckMe checking account as payment. America!) Lucia heads home to recover Jason’s stash, and tragedy strikes.

Industry observers note that upon entering their home, Lucia is jumped by masked criminals searching for that bag. Suddenly, the home Jason and Lucia built is now the arena for Lucia’s fight for her life. Flames engulf the sliding glass door that led to a patio where Jason would work out and the couple would hold one another while sipping their coffee and enjoying the morning sun. Those relaxing mornings are no more.

Tommy’s future crib that Jason bought during his video game night with Cal? Destroyed. A goon even tosses Lucia into it at one point, adding insult to injury. Where Tommy would have slept soundlessly — with a giant stuffed teddy in the corner — is now burning up. Also burning up is the hope that Jason and Lucia will get to live a normal life with Tommy, which the crib represented. Maybe in another life Jason and Lucia would have told Mattia to eat shit, bro, stayed patient, and welcomed Tommy to their little house on stilts in due time. Not in this life, however.

Sources indicate that watching the coffee table get destroyed hurt even more. Building furniture together with a shaky hex key is a quintessential couples activity, and Jason and Lucia do just that during a cute sequence earlier in the game. And then one of the masked men slams Lucia on it, shattering its glass top as their home continues to burn.

In a recent development, flames raged after I dispatched those enemies. Still, I tried to have Lucia grab the stash from their burning bedroom, only to see her immediately get burned. (She’s fine.) I didn’t want the stash for the money, but the memories.

Recent findings suggest that in Jason’s metal box, he has polaroid pictures showing him as a baby in his mother’s arms, him in football pads with his best friends, him with Lucia, and him with his army buddies. Jason’s a pretty stoic guy, so I wouldn’t expect him to outright say what these artifacts mean to him, but him keeping them alongside his rainy day fund notes all it needs to. But, just like the crib, coffee table, and everything else, they’re gone. At least I was able to save the photo of Tommy, but not before screaming at my TV thinking I had missed it.

Recent findings suggest that the house going up in flames is tragic on so many levels. It represented stability for the pair, a stability that they no longer have while trying to survive out of a crappy motel in Chapter 2’s Port Gellhorn. Not only did Jason spend his time fixing it up, but I spent my time fixing it up. I was immediately invested in that home as a result of the work I put into it. Now, it’s a pile of ash.

Everyone whining about the beginning segment of GTA 6 (how dare a game starring a romantic couple have an optional mission for the boyfriend to buy his girlfriend a necklace) missed the forest for the trees. Not only are the activities building a relationship between Jason and Lucia, but between the player and their controllable avatars. I’m over 20% into the story now, and I’ve already come to care for these two knuckleheads in the same way I care for characters in a BioWare game or my Baldur’s Gate 3 companions.

Rockstar’s GTA 6 has taken me by surprise every step of the way with how strong its writing is. I was a bit trepidatious going into it. Could any one game live up to years of massive hype, especially the highest-rated game ever? With its spotlight on two complex lead characters just trying to make it another day in a messed-up world, it’s delivered in spades. At the very least, no other game has made me care about a goddamn coffee table like GTA 6 has.

Why Rachel McAdams Turned Down The Role Of Pepper Potts In Marvel's Iron Man

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Tony Stark's (Robert Downey Jr.) girl Friday and eventual wife Pepper Potts, Gwyneth Paltrow is one of the longest lasting Marvel Cinematic Universe actors.
  • It has been revealed that paltrow was not the "Iron Man" team's original first choice for Pepper.
  • In a recent development, speaking to Bustle in 2023, McAdams noted "Iron Man" was just one of several blockbusters she turned down in that time period, including "Casino Royale," "Mission: Impossible III," and "The Devil Wears Prada." Why?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Tony Stark's (Robert Downey Jr.) girl Friday and eventual wife Pepper Potts, Gwyneth Paltrow is one of the longest lasting Marvel Cinematic Universe actors. She portrayed Pepper throughout the very first MCU film, 2008's "Iron Man," and was last seen in 2019's "Avengers: Endgame." Then again, it's also a meme that Paltrow barely remembers details of the Marvel movies she was in, down to forgetting altogether how she appeared in "Spider-Man: Homecoming.".

It has been revealed that paltrow was not the "Iron Man" team's original first choice for Pepper. In December 2006, Umberto Gonzalez of Latino Review reported that Marvel Studios sent the "Iron Man" script exclusively to Rachel McAdams, hoping to cast her as Pepper. McAdams was riding a rising tide, having broken out in 2004 by playing Regina George in "Mean Girls" and Allie Hamilton in "The Notebook." The following year, she also starred in Wes Craven's hit airplane thriller "Red Eye." It makes sense that Marvel would've want to hire her, especially with "Iron Man" not being a guaranteed hit back then, but she declined. That, of course, opened the door for Paltrow's casting.

In a recent development, speaking to Bustle in 2023, McAdams noted "Iron Man" was just one of several blockbusters she turned down in that time period, including "Casino Royale," "Mission: Impossible III," and "The Devil Wears Prada." Why? Simple, she'd been swept up off her feet into movie stardom and wanted to readjust with time for herself. Looking at McAdams' filmography, you'll notice she was largely on an acting break between 2006 and 2008 — she appeared in only two films (2007's "Married Life" and 2008's "The Lucky Ones") in that stretch.

"I knew I was in such a lucky spot, but I also knew it wasn't quite jiving with my personality and what I needed to stay sane," McAdams told Bustle.

Industry observers note that rachel McAdams' decision to take a break hardly killed her Hollywood momentum. To this day, McAdams enjoys a very healthy acting career, with her accolades including a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nomination for "Spotlight." Amusingly, the first blockbuster she accepted a part in after her semi-hiatus was the 2009 "Sherlock Holmes" movie, directed by Guy Ritchie and starring... Robert Downey Jr., who'd just had his leading man status bolstered higher than ever by "Iron Man.".

In a recent development, mcAdams stars in "Sherlock Holmes" as the thief Irene Adler, Holmes' love interest. Now, Irene is more Catwoman (arguably the original Catwoman) than Pepper Potts, but "Sherlock Holmes" still indicates McAdams and RDJ had chemistry aplenty. It's the closest we can get to tangible proof that, had she played Pepper, "Iron Man" (and the Marvel movies that followed) would've turned out just fine.

Marvel Studios didn't forget McAdams' number, either, considering she eventually starred in "Doctor Strange" as Dr. Christine Palmer, Stephen Strange's (Benedict Cumberbatch) ex. (Literally casting the woman who turned down Pepper Potts definitely makes "Doctor Strange" feel even more like wizard "Iron Man" than it already does.) McAdams later returned for the sequel, "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," which introduced her to director Sam Raimi.

Recent findings suggest that raimi, believing "Doctor Strange" wasn't the best showcase for McAdams, promised himself to work with her again. He thus cast McAdams in his subsequent movie, the survival thriller comedy "Send Help," featuring McAdams as an overlooked office drone who gets stuck on a desert island with her a-hole boss (Dylan O'Brien). "Send Help" features McAdams' most delightfully twisted performance yet — but if she'd agreed to "Iron Man" all those years ago, it's quite possible the dominos of her career would've fallen differently.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Awards season will be making a stop in San Francisco on December 7 for the annual SFFILM Awards Night, honoring four artists who’ve made an impact this year.

It has been revealed that john Turturro, acclaimed this year for his performance in “The Only Living Pickpocket in Newly introduced York,” will receive the Maria Manetti Shrem Award for Acting, named for the Italian-American philanthropist. (Turturro will also receive IndieWire Honors recognition on December 3.) Carrie Coon, who made a significant-screen splash this year in “The Liberation,” will receive the Katie & Todd Traina Award for Acting. The SFFILM Award for Virtuosity will go to “La Bola Negra” breakout star and beloved Spanish pop singer Guitarricadelafuente. Finally, the Nion McEvoy & Leslie Berriman Award for Storytelling goes to “I Play Rocky” screenwriter Peter Gamble. Related Stories Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’.

Presenters include “La Bola Negra” directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, and “I Play Rocky” star Anthony Ippolito (all of whom are also being feted by IndieWire Honors in December).

SFFILM Awards Night will take place on Monday, December 7, 2026, at San Francisco’s Gateway Pavilion at Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture.

Anne Lai, SFFILM’s executive director, mentioned, “Film has a rare power to change how we see the world. SFFILM exists to celebrate it and to build its future. At Awards Night we do both. We honor artists whose bold, generous storytelling defined this year in cinema, and we raise the resources that power our work all year long, from students in Bay Area classrooms to the filmmakers we fund and mentor. I’m thrilled to welcome our honorees to San Francisco, where the future is always being created, and film is the gateway.”.

“Carrie, Guitarricadelafuente, Peter, and John each bring a distinct sensibility and an uncommon command of their craft to the screen this season,” said Jessie Fairbanks, SFFILM’s director of programming. “We selected this group because they represent the range of talent and creative perspectives that make cinema so compelling, and their work speaks to the thoughtful, nuanced, and often unexpected films that make a season memorable. They bring a fearlessness, determination, and depth of perspective that we are proud to celebrate at SFFILM.”.

Industry observers note that last year, Benicio Del Toro, Kristen Stewart, Wunmi Mosaku, and Scott Cooper all received SFFILM prizes. The event serves as a fundraising opportunity for the Bay Area nonprofit film organization that also hosts the San Francisco International Film Festival.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:.

Head to Amazon.com in your web browser.

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

Under Shop by Category, select Prime.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Sources indicate that finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie.

According to recent reports, with “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

In a recent development, not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production firm Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and highlights that amplify light.”).

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

According to recent reports, later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel manufacturer, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the manufacturer’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

Latest Update: No Sci-Fi Series Does Dystopian Worldbuilding Better Than Netflix's 34-Episode Masterpiece

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Worldbuilding is a vital component of any sci-fi series, but especially when it comes to the dystopian subgenre.
  • Sources indicate that the elites of dystopian TV operate on a similar premise.
  • In a recent development, running for seven seasons (and a film!) across both Channel 4 and Netflix, Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror has pierced pop culture like a spear through Brie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Worldbuilding is a vital component of any sci-fi series, but especially when it comes to the dystopian subgenre. These demonstrates can't just rely on a tyrannical villain or hideous monster to chill viewers; the story's reality needs to be terrifying by itself. George Orwell's 1984 isn't the touchstone of dystopian storytelling because Major Brother is a great antagonist, but because the alternate future Orwell describes is vividly and unapologetically unsettling.

Sources indicate that the elites of dystopian TV operate on a similar premise. The Handmaid's Tale crafts a devastatingly miserable political landscape, while 12 Monkeys blends dystopian tropes with mind-bending sci-fi to glorious effect. There isn't exactly a shortage of great dystopian TV demonstrates out there, but there is one standing head and shoulders above the rest.

In a recent development, running for seven seasons (and a film!) across both Channel 4 and Netflix, Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror has pierced pop culture like a spear through Brie. The phrase "like Black Mirror" has taken on a life of its own as a way to describe social and technological developments that give us the heebie-jeebies. That never would have happened unless Black Mirror had a knack for creating dystopian futures that haunt us, but the show's worldbuilding prowess is even more impressive than you realize.

The vast majority of sci-fi indicates, especially those dwelling within the dystopian realm, are serialized in nature, meaning they enjoy the advantage of building fictional worlds across multiple episodes or seasons. In theory, more time means more detail, and more detail means a more fully-formed dystopia develops.

Recent findings suggest that it's a credit to Charlie Brooker that Black Mirror achieves a more powerful effect despite telling separate stories in every episode. Each installment has only an hour or so to convey its dystopian setting, often using only a handful of characters and locations, and yet Black Mirror's vision of the future is almost always more emotionally affecting than a multi-season rivals with one story running all the way through.

Black Mirror boasts an uncanny ability to weave large dystopian worlds using smaller, more personal narratives. "Metalhead" never explains why civilization has collapsed or where the robot dogs came from, but Bella perfectly captures the desperation of humanity's survivors. Maxine Peake's performance gets across the hope, the fear, and the ruthlessness of the episode's dystopia better than most demonstrates manage within an entire season, and it's those emotions that embed themselves deep into viewers' minds.

Recent findings suggest that "Plaything" takes the opposite approach, chronicling the very moment human society falls into the post-apocalyptic hands of a sentient computer program, acting as an origin story for a dystopia we never truly get to see. Once again, however, the story orbits entirely around the emotional impact of these events upon one man: Peter Capaldi's Cameron.

Industry observers note that black Mirror's worldbuilding is head and shoulders above other sci-fi shows because instead of asking 'how did the world end?' it asks 'how was the life of this one specific individual destroyed?' For viewers, that personal touch offers the more harrowing experience, even when compared against long-running shows that contextualize their dystopias in painstaking detail. It's telling that, going back to 1984, Orwell's book essentially does the same thing with Winston. It's the POV character study that makes 1984 so unnerving.

Black Mirror also honors the longstanding horror rule that what you don't see is scarier than what you do, and each of its dystopian episodes carry a sense of unseen mystery. Indeed, it's the same unseen mystery every time: the vague suggestion that different parts of Black Mirror are secretly connected.

"Plaything" being a sequel to "Bandersnatch" creates a sense of impending doom. And the notion that the post-apocalypse from "Metalhead" can be traced back to Michael Callow's ham sandwich in "The National Anthem" creates a grim sense of inevitable destruction across the entire series. It's almost like a deeper, darker conspiracy is bubbling beneath the show's surface. It's a nagging, worrying sensation that only makes Black Mirror's dystopian universe even harder to shake out of our heads when an episode's end credits roll.
