📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix is home to an incredible and vast library of content, but one hidden gem boasts a stellar cast and a gripping story that is the perfect thing to binge over the weekend. When looking for a tense and thrilling series to watch, and avoiding something a little too chunky that will take weeks to work through, a limited series is often a perfect compromise.

With a narrative that has a beginning, middle, and end, without overstaying its welcome, limited series' create some of the best and most complete stories on TV and streaming alike, and Harlan Coben's novels have lent themselves to creating some of the absolute best.

Industry observers note that while several of Harlan Coben's best stories have ended up with adaptations on competing platforms like Prime Video, a particularly powerful series has gone under the radar with I Will Find You somehow managing to pass most people by when it was initially released in June 2026. But don't let that make you think that the quality of this series is anything less than excellent.

According to recent reports, I Will Find You tells the story of a man by the name of David Burroughs, who has been locked away in a prison cell for the crime of having murdered his son. However, when a young woman arrives at the prison with evidence to suggest David's son might be alive, David makes a daring escape and sets out on a mission to find his son.

The stakes are incredibly high, with David on the run, and the prospect of finding his son at the end of the line, while law enforcement hunt him down, and his likelihood of being locked up for life manages to go up and up with every passing moment while searching for his son, who also happens to be the very proof that he never belonged in prison in the first place.

The series is tense, pacy, and pulls the audience along on a thrill ride that features more than a few surprises and delights, as well as some more confronting and emotional beats as the story plays out. Overall, I Will Find You is a stunning piece of work that deserves to find its audience.

Sources indicate that building on the compelling narrative, excellent direction and twisty writing of the series, the show also manages to pull in a whole host of the biggest and best talent in Hollywood. From Avatar's Sam Worthington in the leading role, to Severance's Britt Lower, to Milo Ventimiglia, Erin Richards, Chi McBride, Aaron Ashmore, and Clancy Brown to name a few, this series is stacked.

And not only do these incredible stars light up the screen due to their recognizable faces, but they put their all into this story, and help to create something that delivers genuine emotion and intensity, alongside electric chemistry between the cast, and remarkable beats that are worthy of recognition and praise.

On top of that, the quality of these actors also lends endorsement to the quality of the series, as many of these talented individuals are at the top of their games, and often only invest their time and effort into stories and characters they believe in. That can be felt in each episode of I Will Find You, and it goes a long way to establishing how impactful and meaningful this series is.

Ultimately, though, the story is the key to whether or not this series is worth diving into, and thanks to the incredible guidance and leadership of showrunner Robert Hull, this is another masterclass in adapting the works of Harlan Coben that balances drama, tension, and mystery in a way that is deeply satisfying.

Not only does the story keep things remarkably tight, as it moves swiftly through the plot and makes every one of the eight episodes meaningful and essential to the wider narrative, but it also carefully unwraps a core mystery, layer by layer, throughout the series in a way that is so evidently intentional and deliberate and effective.

Like many of Coben's works, this story manages to pique interests early and fast, while also keeping those watching on the edge of their seats until the end. With all of that in mind, I Will Find You is an incredible series that stands out among a sea of thrillers in a way that is getting increasingly rare, and it deserves more love.

The Official Chronology and Reading Order of Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1268 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that brandon Sanderson's Cosmere is a multi-genre shared literary universe that has been going on since 2005.
  • The Cosmere is planned to be a multi-decade event, and is not expected to conclude anytime soon.
  • The great thing about the Cosmere is that it's engineered to feature multiple entry points — you can generally pick it up from any series or stand-alone story you want and still understand things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that brandon Sanderson's Cosmere is a multi-genre shared literary universe that has been going on since 2005. The premise is that thousands of years ago, in a far-away galaxy, a god known as Adonalsium shattered into 16 pieces called Shards. These Shards found their way to different planets in the galaxy, imbuing them with unique magic systems. Each stand-alone story or series is set on its own planet, with each world varying greatly in terms of culture, ecology, and geography. Yet, they do all connect in some way or another.

The Cosmere is planned to be a multi-decade event, and is not expected to conclude anytime soon. Right now, it consists of 33 entries, including short stories, novellas, novels, graphic novels, and even children's picture books. 33 stories to read is quite overwhelming at first glance, so if you've been looking for a place to start, look no further, because this is the definitive chronology and reading order of the Cosmere.

The great thing about the Cosmere is that it's engineered to feature multiple entry points — you can generally pick it up from any series or stand-alone story you want and still understand things. Sanderson's debut novel, and the first Cosmere novel to be released, was Elantris in 2005, which many fans use as an entry point to the universe. However, seasoned fans do not recommend going this route, as Sanderson's writing is less refined. Instead, many fans suggest picking up the first era of Mistborn as an entry point, as it is more accessible, enticing, easier to read, and generally more exciting.

Sources indicate that however, another viable entry point is the White Sand graphic novel. Originally, White Sand was released as a trilogy, but the canon version is the omnibus version, which includes the original three plus an additional prologue sequence. While a lot of fans don't like White Sand as a story, it is a perfectly good graphic novel and highly crucial to the overall Cosmere. As it right now stands, White Sand is also the first story in the chronology, occurring before Elantris.

Industry observers note that if you really wanted to, though, you could start with Warbreaker, The Stormlight Archive, or any other stand-alone novel, but beginning with White Sand, Elantris, or Mistborn definitely grants a more streamlined approach and makes it easier to hop from one story to the next without needing to jump back and forth through the chronology. On his official website, Sanderson actually recommends reading the books in release order if in doubt, which is a crystal-clear recommendation that doesn't convolute things more than necessary.

The "main" saga of the Cosmere begins with era one of Mistborn. This is followed by the stand-alone novel Warbreaker, which serves as a necessary prequel to The Stormlight Archive. Incidentally, this is what comes next, as the first arc of Stormlight occurs between the two eras of Mistborn. In fact, the final novel in Stormlight's first arc provides a smooth liaison to the second era of Mistborn.

Industry observers note that both of these series consist of multiple novels, as well as various short stories and novellas, which typically serve to fill the gaps between the main novels. Some recommend only reading the short stories or novels after you've finished the main novels in the series, but this isn't strictly necessary: they can be read in the order they chronologically occur, as well.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

According to recent reports, you belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

According to recent reports, "Hoid's Travails" is the informal name given to a trilogy of "Secret Projects" that Sanderson wrote while in quarantine. These three novels are Tress of the Emerald Sea, Yumi and the Nightmare Painter, and The Fires of December, which just came out for backers and is expected to arrive in bookstores soon. This series is more a loose collection of stand-alone novels, each taking place on a different, minor world, with Hoid narrating the story. Other secret projects include The Sunlit Man and Isles of the Emberdark, though these are distinct entities from Hoid's Travails.

According to recent reports, the Sunlit Man absolutely has to be read after Stormlight, or readers will find themselves completely and utterly devoid of context. Also note that when it comes to Isles of the Emberdark, a revised version of the novella Sixth of the Dusk is fully integrated with the novel, so, assuming you read Isles of the Emberdark, Sixth of the Dusk can safely be skipped outright. There are also four picture books, dubbed "Hoid's Storybook Collection," that have just come out, best read alongside The Stormlight Archive because Hoid tells three of the stories to characters from that series, and the picture books are just illustrated versions of his fables. The fourth picture book, The ChasmFriends Get a Pet!, is non-canon and can safely be ignored, although it is a fun read.

Other than that, all that's left is the novellas The Emperor's Soul and Shadows for Silence: In the Forests of Hell. Truth be told, you can read these stand-alone tales pretty much whenever you want. They do have a place in the chronology, but you ultimately won't miss out on anything if you read them first or last. Note that most novellas and short stories can be found contained in a single volume, titled Arcanum Unbounded: The Cosmere Collection.

With the information available, it can be inferred that this is the chronological order of all Cosmere stories, including graphic novels, novels, novellas, picture books, and short stories:.

Industry observers note that this chronology is based on a combination of fan speculation and official word from Sanderson himself, though it is by no means the final timeline. As the Cosmere evolves, this timeline is subject to change. Buckle up, because it's been estimated that Sanderson is only about halfway done with the saga, if not a little bit less than that. It is known that a forthcoming series titled Dragonsteel is set to be the first chronological entry, even before White Sand, while the forthcoming final era of Mistborn is set to be the conclusion to the universe itself. These releases are pretty far away, however, so there's no need to worry about those just yet.

All of this can seem overwhelming, but if it's any reassurance, there really is no "right" way to read the books. Obviously, make sure you read each individual series in order, but other than that, you basically have free rein when it comes to entry and exit points.

  • Recent findings suggest that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • Recent findings suggest that website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all people, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

Recent findings suggest that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Recent findings suggest that website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all people, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

In a recent development, with a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but notes you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

Recent findings suggest that the finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a newly introduced window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Industry observers note that everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

It has been revealed that for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

In a recent development, maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a massive family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Industry observers note that bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

Industry observers note that it looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It promptly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

It has been revealed that juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

It has been revealed that A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that swiftly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

It has been revealed that the new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, baldur’s Gate 3 is returning, but not in the form of a sequel or another playable adventure. The next official story set in Larian Studios’ celebrated Forgotten Realms setting will arrive as a fantasy novel focused on Shadowheart, the cleric whose complicated relationship with faith, memory, and the goddess Shar made her one of the game’s most memorable companions and a fan favorite.

Titled Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart, the book is written by World Fantasy Award-winning author Tasha Suri and is scheduled for publication on June 8, 2027, with preorders already available (Pre-order your copy here). Rather than continuing the party’s story after the game, the novel travels into Shadowheart’s past, following her life inside Shar’s secretive religious order and a murder investigation in Baldur’s Gate.

Baldur's Gate 3 is available to pre-order now through this link.

It has been revealed that the novel begins with Shadowheart serving Shar, the goddess associated with darkness and loss. Her faith is rooted in the belief that surrendering memories is a route to power, and she lives beneath Baldur’s Gate in an underground church. That setting gives the story room to examine the beliefs and rituals that shaped her before the events of the game, rather than simply revisiting familiar adventures.

Her place in the order changes when one of its members is found murdered in the city’s affluent Upper City. Shadowheart is assigned to investigate alongside fellow acolytes, taking her beyond the underground community she knows. The case places the secretive church in contact with a wealthy district whose polished appearance conceals plenty of its own dangerous secrets, making the city itself part of the mystery.

Sources indicate that the investigation brings three companions into the story: Mirie, an ambitious Griefguard; Caldan, a cynical propagandist; and Nocturne, a charming quartermaster whose motives Shadowheart has reason to doubt. Their different roles suggest that the mystery will involve more than identifying a killer, putting questions of loyalty, influence, and trust alongside the central crime.

Recent findings suggest that as Shadowheart follows the evidence, she encounters unfamiliar temptations and begins to question the comforts offered by her faith. The official premise frames the murder as a test of both her investigative judgment and her devotion to Shar. It also sets up a more intimate character story, exploring the convictions she holds before players meet her in Baldur’s Gate 3 and learn how much her past has shaped her.

The book’s precise place in the game’s timeline has not been fully explained in the announcement. However, its focus on Shadowheart’s service to Shar and her life in the underground church establishes it as a prequel focused on her earlier experiences. Readers should not mistake it for a direct adaptation of her branching storyline or a continuation of the game’s multiple possible endings.

Recent findings suggest that shadowheart’s novel also joins a growing collection of stories expanding the role-playing game beyond the screen. Astarion previously received a prequel novel by T. Kingfisher, while character-focused comics have added more material to the setting. These releases give fans additional opportunities to explore the personalities and history behind some of the game's most recognizable companions.

According to recent reports, the franchise is also moving toward television: HBO is developing an official Baldur’s Gate series from The Last of Us co-creator Craig Mazin, expected to take place after Baldur’s Gate 3. Unlike that upcoming adaptation, Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart will revisit the character's earlier life. The novel arrives June 8, 2027, offering fans another official way to return to the Forgotten Realms.

Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • Sources indicate that macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the manufacturer’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Sources indicate that macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It has been revealed that it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

I’m a major fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy owners at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, people had to wait until it “just worked.”.

According to recent reports, apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an update, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

In a recent development, another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

Recent findings suggest that it’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech users may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Sources indicate that is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

It has been revealed that bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes is like few other comic strips. Sure, it's funny, with a decade's worth of moments following an unaging Calvin and his stuffed tiger Hobbes as they navigate their suburban life. Despite his young age, Calvin is smarter than other kids. He's a boy who lives in his imagination and loves to cause chaos.

According to recent reports, his intelligence, however, has also led to many heartbreaking strips. Watterson, like Charles M. Schulz did with Peanuts, took his own grown-up anxieties and shared them through the confused eyes of an innocent child. Calvin is often happy and confident, so it's absolutely gut-wrenching to see him sad in these eight strips.

Sources indicate that calvin only has one friend in the world, and he isn't real. He could have an actual human friend, his next-door neighbor, Susie, but because she's a girl, Calvin rejects the idea nearly every time. To him, girls are gross and aren't allowed in the club he has with Hobbes. Deep down, he really does like her, though, as shown in how Hobbes is smitten with her, and he feels bad about how mean he is.

He won't tell her that. All Susie wants is a friend. She's just as lonely as Calvin is, and for her effort, she's constantly rejected and made fun of. In this strip, she lets her anger out. She can't believe how he treats her and tries to tell herself that she doesn't need him as a friend. Then comes the final panel of Susie playing by herself. It's not enough.

Industry observers note that calvin has a complicated relationship with his parents. He genuinely loves them, and there are some adorably sweet strips of them together as a loving family. With his wild imagination and non-stop energy, he also drives them nuts, especially his dad. Calvin's father is a man of rules. Most often, he wants to just be left alone, with all of his advice being about building character.

In a recent development, usually, he takes it and doesn't react much when Calvin annoys him. In this strip, that's not the case. When Calvin breaks his binoculars, he goes off, screaming his lungs out in a rage. In a rare moment, Calvin's confidence breaks, and he cries, leaving his father shaken. He knows he has crossed a line and hurt his son.

Sources indicate that without ever explicitly saying it, Calvin and Hobbes portrays its lead as a lonely boy with no friends. He lives in his imagination, a place he can mold into anything he wants it to be. This strip demonstrates that part of his loneliness comes from his home life. Mom and Dad aren't bad people by any means, but they're also so wrapped up in their own lives that they forget to pay attention to their son.

Here, in a stunningly drawn Sunday strip, Calvin tries to zap his dull parents into something more interesting by turning them into monsters. When they dismiss his antics, an upset Calvin goes upstairs and stares out his window. He turns his world into a far-off planet in his mind. Instead of making him feel better, the visuals only deepen his despair. Far off is exactly how he feels.

It has been revealed that four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

According to recent reports, you have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

It has been revealed that calvin mocks so many things. Pretty much every human — and their confusing behavior — frustrates him. You'll never find him doing that with animals, though. We can see how much he loves all creatures, great and small, through his friendship with Hobbes. His stuffed tiger is his everything.

It has been revealed that in this strip, it's only two simple panels that say it all by saying so little. Calvin is bewildered by how mean people are. It'll be okay, because Hobbes is here, and animals are a comfort. Calvin feels how many of us do. If we're having a bad day, all we have to do is hug our dog or cat, and we instantly feel better.

Calvin and Hobbes is not afraid to look at death, as these next few examples will show. Here, with the added panels of a Sunday entry, we get an extended conversation between two friends after they find a dead bird. Rather than being overly upset, Calvin is in awe of how beautiful and delicate life can be.

It has been revealed that we're all going to die, and it could happen at any moment. Just as upsetting is knowing that the fear of death causes us to do all we can to avoid thinking about it. Calvin can't stop his thoughts. His only hope is that he'll figure it out when he becomes an adult. Bill Watterson knows he won't.

It has been revealed that calvin and Hobbes' most painful strips are a story told over several days when Calvin and Hobbes find a sick raccoon while out exploring. Desperate to save it, Calvin gets his parents to take it in. Surely the grownups can fix it and make everything okay.

They can't. Here, his dad must tell Calvin that the raccoon has passed away. Gone is the father who gets easily upset or completely ignores his son. He puts his arm around Calvin, being thoughtful with his words about how the raccoon didn't die alone. Calvin accepts this, but he can't let go. That vulnerable, innocent animal got into his very soul.

In the same raccoon storyline, Calvin is processing his grief about the dead raccoon. He's no longer crying his eyes out. Now he's working through the wise words his mother shared with him. Like his dad previously, she hasn't dismissed her son for caring. She also hasn't sugar-coated anything or acted like she has all the answers.

In a recent development, all living things are born and die. The only thing we can do is try our best despite knowing so very little about our own world. Nothing makes sense, and that makes sense to Calvin. Death is unavoidable. Still, Hobbes is not allowed to die. Calvin needs his imaginary friend, who will live on as long as his owner believes in him.

According to recent reports, another expanded Sunday comic takes us into Calvin's greatest fear: reality. He lives in his mind with Hobbes for a reason. Calvin doesn't understand his world or his place in it. It's much safer to pretend in a world he can control. At school, that becomes harder because it's the only place where he can't take Hobbes with him.

Sources indicate that there, Calvin is on his own. No one is there to help him when math makes him feel dumb. No tiger is there to maul his bully to death. At home, the commitments don't end. Whether it's homework, dinner, a bath, or going to bed early, the boredom of everyday life doesn't stop. When his mother kisses him and talks about tomorrow being another big day, it brings no relief. Is this all there is? Without Hobbes by his side in this rare strip, he can't take it.

Early 2027 is going to be a surprisingly important period for the iPhone, and it's all thanks to the iPhone 18. Rather than release the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 in the fall, both phones have are reportedly launching early next year — with rumors claiming they'll arrive alongside iPhone 18e in the spring.

Industry observers note that now that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo are out in the world, the rumors are starting to reveal more about the three upcoming iPhones. The latest leaks suggest that we may even see some design changes, especially in the look and feel of the rear cameras.

First look at the iPhone 18 Air and iPhone 18 dummy units. The biggest change is the iPhone 18 Air, which now features two rear cameras instead of one, while the standard iPhone 18 retains a design similar to the iPhone 17. https://t.co/MdOVuwPlm3November 20, 2026.

According to dummy units leaked by Sonny Dickson, the iPhone 18 will look more or less the same as the iPhone 17, complete with the two vertical camera lenses on the back. The iPhone Air 2 will apparently be similar to the original iPhone Air, albeit with an additional camera lens.

Sources indicate that that's right, the iPhone Air 2 could fix one of its biggest concerns and take some visual inspiration from the iPhone Duo in the process. However, the camera bar on the dummy units does stretch across the entire width of the phone, whereas the iPhone Duo only covers around three quarters of a single side.

It has been revealed that it's likely that this is an ultrawide camera, which should mean the Air 2's camera capabilities will be closer to that of the iPhone 18 rather than the (presumably) single-camera iPhone 18e. That's even more likely when you remember that telephoto lenses take up a lot of space, and considering the slimline nature of the iPhone Air, that space is already at a premium.

Of course, we do need to be wary of all sorts of leaks and claims online, especially since Dickson recently posted alleged Galaxy S27 Ultra dummy units that contradict every rumor we've heard so far. So take these designs with a grain of salt.

Industry observers note that while the iPhone 18 may not be getting any changes (if Dickson's dummy units are to be believed), the same may not be true for the iPhone 18e. Engadget claims to have seen CAD files of the phone, and apparently it could be coming with a square-shaped camera bump.

The site also claims that other CAD images showcase the iPhone Air 2 with a second rear camera, and an iPhone 18 that is mostly unchanged from the iPhone 17.

Engadget doesn't provide any of the CAD images, or even renders of what the redesigned camera bump might look like. However, Engadget says it looks like the square module on the back of the iPad Pro M5, which gives us some idea of what this alleged redesign could look like — assuming the claims are actually true.

Industry observers note that personally, I'm a little bit skeptical, on account of the fact that we don't actually see the CAD images that are referenced in the initial report. Likewise, I'm not so sure Apple would redesign the iPhone 18e's camera bump considering the E-series cameras have so far been solo camera lenses with a pinhead-sized microphone and LED flash. A boxed-in bump seems like an odd design choice.

It has been revealed that plus, that redesign wouldn't really work if the iPhone 18 does stick with the same design as before. I'd be more inclined to believe reports that the iPhone 18 would get a square camera bump, but we don't know if such a thing will happen. Dickson's dummy unit, and Engadget's own reporting, suggest not.

We'll find out for sure next year, and current rumors suggest that these three phones will arrive in February or March.

According to recent reports, our favorite amplifier at the moment is the Denon AVR-X4800H. It's an excellent performer with loads of great features, and doesn't cost as much as similar options. or if you need something that handle any format you throw at it, I'd recommend the Marantz Cinema 50.

It has been revealed that A sonic tour de force, the X4800H is a home theater amplifier with long-term appeal. The provision of a full board of 8K/4K 120Hz HDMI inputs, and coverage of all the significant home cinema sound formats, ensures that this Denon amp will partner any display or source you might acquire for a long time to come.

According to recent reports, it's not the smallest box, but that's because it's fill with loads of amplification tech, supporting nine channels for massive surround sound or an Atmos system. The screen on the front makes it easy to read what mode its in, and then there's an easy setup mode when you plug it into your TV or projector. From there, you can setup all of the different settings and features to get the most out of your receiver.

It has been revealed that the sound is powerful enough to make the experience feel almost physical. While Denon rates on-board power at 9x 125W (into 8 Ohms) / 200W (into 6 Ohms), it sounds rather more muscular than that.

You'll get the most out of this amplifier while watching movies, especially those with detailed sound effects and soundtracks. But this also makes it a great companion for music, with your favorite tracks coming out of the two-channel stereo sounding light and agile, with immersive 3D audio mixes.

In a recent development, the Marantz Cinema 50 is one of the most future-proof home theater amps we've seen. The connectivity on offer is truly impressive with 8K and 4K 120Hz support, 6 HDMI inputs plus three outputs, and an impressive auto calibration system.

In our 5.1.2 configuration, there were no sonic gaps or dips with any kind of content, just a totally immersive listening experience.

When testing models for inclusion in our best AV receivers page, we play a range of media, including movies, music and games, to evaluate overall sound quality performance.

We also test any companion software that may come with an AV receiver, and factor in how easy it is to set up and use each receiver with a reference speaker system. Other features we consider include the different kinds of connectivity options, all of which determine how well it will work with your home entertainment setup.

We also take into account power output, the number of supported audio channels and subwoofer outputs, and available processing software for decoding movie soundtracks as well as their ability to handle music sources — all factors that greatly affect how each speaker will sound in your living room.

An AV receiver is an amplifier that's designed for home cinema and movie watching. You plug it into your TV with an HDMI cable, and then it takes the audio signal, and processes it for separate speakers. You need to have speakers for an AV receiver to work — it's a kind of go-between device.

According to recent reports, you could have as many speakers as you like, although there's a minimum of two. Everything from a normal stereo (two speakers) up to a much larger surround setup (7.1 and above). It needs to be plugged into the power as well. Remember to budget for speakers with an AV receiver.

Recent findings suggest that this is a major question to ask yourself. Do you have the space for multiple speakers around the room? What kind of watching do you do? Can you budget for more than two speakers?

Recent findings suggest that if the answer to any of those questions is no, then you don't need an AV receiver. I'd argue, in fact, that very few people need an AV receiver — you're much better off with the space-saving capabilities of one of the best soundbars, or the musical chops of a pair of HDMI-enabled powered speakers like the Kanto Ren.

But, if you love watching movies, you've got plenty of space, plenty of budget, and permission from your significant other, then an AV receiver might be just what you've been looking for.

In a recent development, everyone's movie room is different. They're different shapes and have different furniture inside, which can affect the sound of your system. In order to make movies sound their best, no matter what's in your room, manufacturers have built room correction systems that listen to the sound and then compensate for the differences in decor and shape.

Some, like Denon and Yamaha, have made their own room correction systems built into companion apps. Many amplifiers come with microphones to aid the process, and its built into the setup of the device. It's well worth going through the stages, and it can make a significant difference to bass extension and surround sound placement.

Sources indicate that yes, you can! And you most certainly should. Your AVR can be used as the central pillar of a home music system, especially as more and more devices can connect to whole-home music streaming devices. That means you can connect your turntable, CD player, or other devices.

For turntables, there are a couple of things to bear in mind. Some AVRs do not have a built-in phono pre-amp, and so you'll need either a separate device or a TT with a pre-amp built in. If your AVR has a built-in pre-amp, you'll need to make sure you connect your TT to the correct RCA plugs. They'll be labeled "phono.".

Industry observers note that they are good for gaming, though it depends on the types of games you like to play. For immersive RPGs filled with movie-like cutscenes and massive set pieces, you're in for a sonic treat. For fast-paced online shooters, you'll likely want to stick with your gaming headset.

Industry observers note that just make sure that your new AVR and your TV support HDMI 2.1 for the best audio and visual experience possible. That means that 4K120Hz will be supported, along with Variable refresh rates and other game-specific features can be supported.

Industry observers note that if you want to get the most out of the home theater experience, then you should pick up some Atmos speakers for the full effect. Without them, you won't get the spatial audio channels that make the sound come from above you — it's well worth it if you can stump up the cash.

Buying something as complex and multi-talented as an AV receiver can be overwhelming to a casual consumer, so if you’re serious about transforming your sound output into something more theater-like, start educating yourself on the necessities by familiarizing yourself with the things to consider.

Something to know right out of the gate is that most seven-channel AV receivers support a speaker configuration of 5.1.2, which is the standard 5.1 surround layout with two additional height/up-firing speakers. Models that feature nine channels of amplification can be used for either 5.1 with four Dolby height speakers (5.1.4) or 7.1 surround with two height channels (7.1.2). Speaker models such as those in the new Klipsch Reference series could make a great partnership for a home cinema setup, and has several upward-firing height speakers to meet Dolby Amos requirements.

Sources indicate that finding the best AV receiver isn’t just about HDMI inputs. Sure we like plenty of inputs, but the number of outputs is important too, particularly if you plan on running both a flatscreen and a projector in the same room.

If you're considering an AV receiver as a connectivity hub for a music system as well as movies, then be sure to check out our guide to the best turntables for any budget. Many of the receivers available today come with a built-in moving-magnet phono stage to enable vinyl playback from any of the record decks we've tested.

Resolution and frame rate support.

According to recent reports, do you need 8K or High Frame Rate HDMIs? If your AV receiver is unlikely to have a games console connected then the answer is no. In which case there are some great deals to be had on AVRs with regular HDMI 2.0 inputs.

Industry observers note that dolby Atmos compatibility is a given (and by default that means you’ll get DTS:X too), but how many channels do you need? Given the option, 9 channels always trump 7, because it opens up more speaker options such as 5.1.4 or 7.1.2, for example.

It has been revealed that don’t have a full Dolby Atmos home theater loudspeaker setup? Look for a model that offers height virtualization technology, so you can enjoy an immersive audio experience even when you don’t have a full set of physical speakers.

Recent findings suggest that power isn’t just about roof-raising volume, and even if you’re not lucky enough to have a dedicated movie room, a model with massive amplification makes sense. A high power output means an AVR can deliver dynamic transients, and pressure load a space without clipping or strain.

In a recent development, one of the most confusing things about any kind of home cinema system is the surround sound channel numbers you'll often spot on the box. What do they mean, and what do they tell you about the receiver that you're about to buy?

Industry observers note that those numbers denote the channels that are available to use with the receiver. It's broken up into three different sections. The first number is the surround channels. The middle is for subwoofers. The final number is the height channels, for Dolby Atmos and DTS:X.

Sources indicate that say, for example, that you've got a receiver that's got a 7.1.4 surround sound setup. That means you've got seven surround channels that you could use for a centre, left and right stereo, two side surrounds, and then a pair of rear surrounds. You've then got a single subwoofer channel.

Finally, you've got four height channels that you can place around the room in predetermined Atmos spots. You can use Atmos testing videos to make sure all your speakers are in the right place.

Whatever they do decide to do, it would be nice to see another Eeveelution in the new Pokémon games, and if I were a betting man, I'd say Flying or Dragon would be the ones that stand out as the most appropriate for what we know about the setting.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that moviegoers eagerly awaiting the return of The Mummy franchise with next year's The Mummy: Book of the Dead can tide themselves over with another fun action-adventure with heart: the streaming smash hit Masters of the Universe.
  • What was interesting about The Mummy was how it veered away from the horror genre of its source material, the original 1932 movie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider. He is an MPA-accredited entertainment journalist and a Tomatometer-approved critic based in the LA area. He graduated from the University of Texas at Austin with a Bachelor of Science in Radio, TV, & Film and a Bachelor of Arts in Theater.

Recent findings suggest that moviegoers eagerly awaiting the return of The Mummy franchise with next year's The Mummy: Book of the Dead can tide themselves over with another fun action-adventure with heart: the streaming smash hit Masters of the Universe. Based on the iconic 1980s Mattel toy line and Filmation animated series, Masters of the Universe wasn't a box office success, but it's finding a much bigger audience on streaming, topping the Nielsen streaming charts after its Prime Video debut. Fans who love high-octane action-adventure stories that are still full of humor, emotion, and genuine stakes, in the vein of The Mummy, will definitely want to check out Masters of the Universe.

What was interesting about The Mummy was how it veered away from the horror genre of its source material, the original 1932 movie. Instead, the 1999 reboot adopted more of an action-adventure, vintage serial movie style, evoking Steven Spielberg's Indiana Jones movies, with the addition of a slightly more modern vibe and voice within the period setting. That imbued The Mummy reboot with a unique and infectious effervescence that makes it so entertaining to watch.

Masters of the Universe follows a similar playbook: an action-adventure movie that takes itself fairly seriously, but still knows how to have fun and not become overly self-serious. That tone aligns perfectly with the source material, especially considering how silly and goofy the Filmation series could be. Thankfully, director Travis Knight updates the original cartoon's humor, aging it up, resulting in a movie that feels fresh and upcoming, but still speaks to the child in you that loves He-Man and the Masters of the Universe.

According to recent reports, not to mention, Masters of the Universe features incredibly charming leads with Nicholas Galitzine as Adam/He-Man and Camila Mendes as Teela, who showcase wonderful chemistry. Their dynamic evokes the sparks that Brendan Fraser and Rachel Weisz created with their romance in The Mummy as Rick O'Connell and Evelyn Carnahan. The movie presents Adam as a comedically inept young man and HR worker who doesn't look or act like the traditional hero. However, Knight and screenwriter Chris Butler excellently craft Adam with depth as someone who yearns to return to his home planet and must become the legendary He-Man to defend it.

True, Masters of the Universe was born from a 1980s toy line, but therein lies the fun. The movie captures the childlike imagination and whimsy of dumping your action figures in a sandbox and letting your imagination unfold. Part of the joy of the vintage toys was rooted in how they were purposefully designed with their own lore, mythology, and history, providing kids with a jumping-off point to create their own stories within Eternia. Travis Knight, who has already proven he works well with similar material such as the Transformers spin-off Bumblebee, and other fantasy adventures such as Kubo and the Two Strings and Wildwood, truly brings the world of Eternia to life onscreen.

It has been revealed that knight imbues every frame with pure joy, awe, and wonderment, with a visual fidelity to the source material that most adaptations of existing IP and comic book superhero movies lack, right down to the colors of characters' costumes. For fans who grew up with Masters of the Universe, it was an absolute joy to see Eternia, Castle Grayskull, Snake Mountain, and many classic characters brought to vivid life onscreen and faithfully resemble their action figure and animated counterparts. When Adam finally held aloft his magic sword and said the words, "I have the power," becoming He-Man, it was a 10/10 moment with no notes. Plus, the movie is beautifully enhanced by wonderful music composed by Daniel Pemberton, with guitar renditions by rock legend Brian May.

In a recent development, although Arnold Vosloo is great as Imhotep in The Mummy movies, sometimes the films focused more on cutting-edge visual effects and Imhotep as a CGI monster than creating a genuine threat and epic cinematic villain. But one area where Masters of the Universe outdoes The Mummy is its antagonist: Skeletor (Jared Leto). Make no mistake, Skeletor is the true star of Masters of the Universe, and the new movie excellently realizes the unparalleled overlord of evil with a mix of great practical costume work and digital effects. The CGI enhancement that realizes Skeletor’s bony visage is executed to perfection.

Leto's performance as Skeletor evokes the Filmation series' version, down to the way he constantly derides his minions. However, the fresh movie still treats Skeletor as a genuine threat despite his maniacal mirth; Leto brings both humorous charisma and genuine menace to Skeletor in a lethal combination. In recent times, it's rare for a major blockbuster to depict a fun villain who unapologetically embraces villainy. So it's great, for once, to have a villain who is evil simply because he enjoys it. Like he says in the movie, "I am the villain. And mmm, does it feel good!".

In a recent development, the Mummy: Book of the Dead will be out in theaters on October 15, 2027. In the meantime, you can check out Masters of the Universe, which is streaming now on Prime Video.

Apple Wallet car keys are about to get a big expansion, with GM launching support for a variety of vehicles across three of its popular brands: Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC.

This fall, GM announced that its long-awaited Apple Wallet car key rollout was finally happening after first being mentioned by Apple in June 2025.

Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC vehicles are all gaining support for storing a digital car key in Apple Wallet.

Per the announcement, a very limited rollout started in late September and into October for select Cadillacs, but it will hit a lot more vehicles in December—including Chevrolet and GMC models.

As seen in the image above, GM is launching car key support for the following vehicles:.

With support for all of these models launching before year’s end, this represents one of the broadest car key expansions of late.

GM also confirms that the rollout “will continue across additional GM vehicles over time.” It says when a vehicle adds car key support, customers will get notified in the ‘What’s Latest’ section of their vehicle’s app.

Industry News: The 5 best all-in-one printers in 2026 for home and office, tested by experts
